seoTitle: Asana Tutorial for Beginners: Task Management Basics
metaDescription: New to Asana? This beginner walkthrough covers creating projects, adding tasks, assigning work, and tracking progress, plus which parts need a paid plan.
intro:
Asana is a project and task management tool built to help teams organize work, assign responsibility, and track progress in one place. For a brand-new user the interface can look busier than it needs to be, with a sidebar, tabs, filters, and views all competing for attention. This guide focuses on the handful of screens you'll live in during your first week: creating a project, filling it with tasks and sections, checking your own workload from My tasks, and adding the fields that turn a plain to-do list into something a team can report on.

Most of this works on Asana's free Personal plan. Two pieces don't: custom fields and Timeline view. Both are covered below since they're common enough that a beginner will run into them fast, but they need Asana's Starter plan or an active free trial, not the permanently free tier.
costNote: Asana's Personal plan is free forever for up to two people and covers projects, tasks, sections, List, Board, and Calendar views, and My tasks. Custom fields (like the Status column in step four) and Timeline view (step six) require the Starter plan, currently around $11 per user per month billed annually, or an active free trial. When a trial ends, expect those two features to stop working until you upgrade.

steps.heading: Start from Browse projects
steps.body: Once you're logged in, the Projects tab in the left sidebar takes you to Browse projects, which lists every project you're a member of along with its owner and portfolio. A brand-new workspace usually has one starter project already in it, often a sample onboarding checklist Asana creates for you to poke around in. The Create project button sits in the top right; below it, Asana also surfaces a few ready-made templates, like a new hire checklist or a meeting agenda tracker, worth a look if you'd rather start from a structure than a blank page.

image.caption: Browse projects lists everything you're a member of, with Create project and a row of starter templates for common workflows.

steps.heading: Build the task list with sections
steps.body: Open a project and you land on its List view, the default and the one most beginners should stick with first. Tasks are grouped into sections, labeled buckets like "Week 1 check-ins" or "Tools & access," and each task carries its own row of columns: Assignee, Due date, and any custom fields you've added. Typing a task name and pressing Add task keeps things moving fast; you fill in the details afterward. The first time you set up a project, Asana also prompts you to pick a default view for the team, List, Board, Calendar, or Timeline, which just decides what people see when they open it, not how the data is stored.

image.caption: A project's List view, with tasks grouped into sections and Asana prompting for a default view for the team.

steps.heading: Check your workload in My tasks
steps.body: My tasks, in the sidebar under Home, pulls together everything assigned to you across every project into one personal list. By default it's grouped into Recently assigned, Do today, Do next week, and Do later, a rough priority order without any setup on your part. This is the screen to open each morning instead of hunting through individual projects. If a task's due date changes or someone assigns you something new, it shows up here immediately, and each row still tells you which project it came from.

image.caption: My tasks collects everything assigned to you into Recently assigned, Do today, Do next week, and Do later groups.

steps.heading: Add custom fields like Status (requires Starter)
steps.body:
Columns beyond Assignee and Due date aren't fixed. Click the + at the end of the column header row to add a custom field. Status is one of the most useful early additions: it lets you mark a task To do, In Progress, or Complete with a colored tag instead of relying on the checkbox alone, which matters once a project has more than a few tasks and you want to scan progress at a glance.

This is one of the two features in this guide that isn't part of Asana's free Personal plan. If the + option is missing or grayed out, that's the plan speaking, not a bug. Fields you do add apply to the whole project, and Asana confirms the change with a small toast in the corner.

steps.heading: Assign owners and set due dates
steps.body: Every task benefits from an assignee and a due date, even in a small team; an unassigned task is a common reason work quietly stalls. Click into the Assignee cell to search teammates by name, and the Due date cell to open a calendar picker. You can set a date range instead of a single day for multi-day work, which is what lets Asana render the task correctly later in Timeline view. Sections can also carry their own owner-function tags, as seen in the sample onboarding project, a lightweight way to show which role, Manager, IT, Engineer, is responsible for a batch of tasks without assigning every single one individually.

steps.heading: Switch views without changing your data (Timeline needs Starter)
steps.body: Along the top of any project sit tabs for List, Board, Timeline, Calendar, and Dashboard, plus a + to add more. These are different lenses on the same tasks, not separate copies: moving a task's due date in Calendar view updates it everywhere else too. Board view turns your sections into Kanban-style columns you can drag cards between, which teams coming from Trello tend to reach for first, and it's included on the free plan. Timeline, which lays tasks out against a calendar bar chart and is worth turning on once a project has dependencies, is the second feature here that needs Starter or a trial.

faq.question: Is Asana free to use?
faq.answer: Yes. The Personal plan is free forever for up to two people and covers List, Board, and Calendar views plus My tasks. Custom fields and Timeline are Starter-plan features, around $11 per user per month billed annually, though a free trial unlocks them temporarily.

faq.question: What's the difference between a project and a section?
faq.answer: A project is the overall container, like "Team onboarding," while sections are groupings inside it, like "Week 1 check-ins" or "Tools & access," that organize related tasks together.

faq.question: How do I see only the tasks assigned to me?
faq.answer: Open My tasks from the sidebar. It automatically pulls in every task assigned to you across all projects and groups them by urgency: Recently assigned, Do today, Do next week, and Do later.

faq.question: Can I add my own columns to a project?
faq.answer: Yes, but it needs Starter or above. Click the + at the end of the column headers in List view to add a custom field such as Status or Priority; on the free Personal plan that option won't be available.

faq.question: Does switching between List, Board, and Timeline change my tasks?
faq.answer: No. All views read from the same underlying tasks, so a change made in one, like updating a due date, shows up immediately in the others. Timeline itself, though, only appears on Starter and above.

faq.question: Will my custom fields disappear if a free trial ends?
faq.answer: They'll stop being usable on a Personal-plan workspace, since custom fields aren't part of that tier. Upgrading to Starter is what keeps them active.

verifiedNote: Click path and screens come from a walkthrough recorded on Asana. My tasks' default grouping (Recently assigned, Do today, Do next week, Do later) matched Asana's own help documentation on re-check. Plan gating was re-checked against asana.com/pricing in September 2026, which is what corrected this guide's earlier claim that nothing in the walkthrough required a paid plan: custom fields and Timeline view both need Starter or an active trial.
